findings.claim: Examiners consistently reward specific, measurable design criteria and penalise vague ones.
findings.truth: No published examiner statement supports this. The defensible point is that a measurable criterion can be tested against the finished product and a vague one cannot.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims or invented mark-scheme behaviour

findings.claim: "Make it more eco-friendly" scores no marks. ... are the types of response examiners credit.
findings.truth: Invented mark-scheme behaviour. Rewritten as a testability point: a named material or process can be checked, a vague aim cannot.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: The cup must be made from food-grade, BPA-free polymer and have no components smaller than 45 mm in any direction to eliminate choking risk.
findings.truth: 45 mm is invented. The small parts test in BS EN 71-1 uses a cylinder of 31.7 mm internal diameter (25.4-57.1 mm depth); a part that fits wholly inside it is a choking hazard for under-3s. Lesson 5 of this same unit gives the 31.7 mm figure correctly, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: BS EN 71-1 small parts cylinder; L5 content_html of this unit

findings.claim: examiners explicitly contrast these two answer types and only award marks for the specific action
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. The spec sets no such rule; the real point is that a named material or process can be tested.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Designing and making principles; house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Safety - standards the product must meet (e.g. CE marking for electrical products).
findings.truth: CE is a conformity mark, not a standard, and UKCA is the Great Britain equivalent introduced in 2021 (CE is still accepted for most goods). Not mark-affecting at GCSE, so left alone.

findings.claim: Examiners reward responses that connect design decisions to outcomes (plus the panel heading "What Examiners Look For").
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Rewritten as direct advice to link a design decision to its outcome.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Under Jony Ive as Chief Design Officer, Apple developed a design philosophy ... iMac G3 (1998), iPod (2001), iPhone (2007).
findings.truth: Ive led industrial design from 1996 and held the title Chief Design Officer only from 2015 to 2019, so the title is anachronistic for the products named. The design attribution itself is right and the title is not examinable.

findings.claim: Examiners reward extended responses on iterative design that show how user feedback informs decisions throughout the process.
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Rewritten as a description of a strong answer.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Writing "the designer used user-centred design" earns one mark at best. ... earns the application marks that lift a response into the higher band.
findings.truth: Invented mark-scheme behaviour. Rewritten to contrast naming a strategy with applying it to the scenario.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims or band wording

findings.claim: Isometric drawing presents a product in three dimensions with all parallel edges drawn at 30 degrees to the horizontal.
findings.truth: In isometric drawing the vertical edges are drawn vertical; only the two sets of horizontal edges are drawn at 30 degrees to the horizontal. The lesson's own glossary entry and knowledge check state the rule correctly, so the body text was the outlier.
findings.evidence: standard isometric construction (BS 8888 / GCSE convention); glossary_terms and knowledge_checks in the same lesson

findings.claim: One-point perspective, where all horizontal lines recede to a single vanishing point, is effective for interiors.
findings.truth: In one-point perspective only the lines running away from the viewer converge on the vanishing point. Horizontal lines parallel to the picture plane stay horizontal, which is what distinguishes one-point from two-point perspective.
findings.evidence: standard perspective construction; the lesson's own two-point description

findings.claim: Examiners expect students to understand that feedback from user testing informs design decisions throughout the process.
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. The statement itself is sound and is kept without the examiner framing.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 point 10 (respond to feedback to identify potential for further development)

findings.claim: The key distinction examiners look for is whether feedback genuinely informs decisions or merely documents what happened.
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim; the distinction is kept as a design point.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Examiners reward evaluations that are specific and evidence-based.
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Rewritten as a description of a good evaluation.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Examiners have identified a recurring error: students describe user testing as useful only because it "improves the final product." ... The examiner-rewarded point is ...
findings.truth: An invented examiner-report finding. No such published report is cited or exists for this qualification. The teaching point survives without the attribution.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims or invented report findings

findings.claim: Examiners explicitly reward feedback that informs decisions throughout the process, not just at the end.
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Rewritten as an instruction to the student.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

summary: Content and answer keys are largely sound: the five named designers and companies match the spec list exactly (Airbus, Apple, James Dyson, Philippe Starck, Matthew Williamson), the Dyson, Juicy Salif and A380 facts check out, no lesson names the board, and all 25 knowledge check keys and every practice mark scheme total are correct. The real problems are one wrong drawing rule (isometric edges at 30 degrees), one wrong perspective rule, an invented 45 mm choking-hazard figure that contradicts lesson 5, and eleven fabricated examiner or mark-scheme claims spread across all five lessons.
